Hatchlings of Crocodylus niloticus emerge from eggs incubated at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] after a developmental period of 90 days [ab = 90 days], a duration that aligns with the protracted incubation characteristic of large-bodied crocodylians. At the moment of emergence, neonates measure approximately 29 cm [Lb = approximately 29 cm] in total length and possess a wet body mass of 70 grams [Wwb = 70 grams], reflecting the substantial residual yolk reserves that sustain them during the initial lecithotrophic phase. These yolk-sac larvae rely entirely on endogenous nutrients for the first several weeks, gradually transitioning to active prey capture as the external yolk mass is resorbed. The substantial investment in each offspring, evident in the relatively large egg size and hatchling mass, is typical for a species that exhibits extensive maternal care, including nest guarding and assisted transport of young to aquatic nursery habitats.

As juveniles progress through the sub-adult stage, growth remains highly dependent on environmental temperature, and this species exhibits one of the most dramatic size dimorphisms among extant crocodylians. Under the thermal regime of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], females typically reach reproductive maturity and begin producing their first egg clutch at 14 years after hatching [tR = 14 years after hatching], a protracted delay that underscores the slow pace of life history in this apex predator. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 155,000 grams [Wwp = 155,000 grams], a threshold reflecting the substantial somatic capital required to sustain reproductive effort. This body size at maturation for females is reached at a total length of approximately 280 cm [Lp = approximately 280 cm], whereas males initiate puberty at a larger size of around 330 cm [Lp = around 330 cm], a divergence consistent with the intense male-male competition for breeding territories that characterizes this species.

The ultimate total length for female Nile crocodiles reaches 427 cm [Li = 427 cm], while males attain a considerably larger asymptotic length of 610 cm [Li = 610 cm], representing one of the most extreme cases of sexual size dimorphism among living reptiles. This divergence in ultimate body size is paralleled by dramatic differences in ultimate wet weight, with females achieving a maximum adult mass of 763,000 grams [Wwi = 763,000 grams] and males reaching approximately 1,090,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,090,000 grams]. The selective pressures driving this dimorphism are multifaceted, encompassing advantages in territory defense, access to larger prey items, and dominance during the breeding season. Males, in particular, invest heavily in somatic growth before initiating reproductive activity, with growth rates remaining elevated well beyond the age at which females have already approached their asymptotic size.

Reproductive output in this species is closely tied to body size, and at a total length of 364 cm, a female Crocodylus niloticus maintained at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] produces approximately 95 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 95 eggs per year], representing a substantial annual fecundity for a reptile of this magnitude. This rate of egg production is among the highest recorded for any crocodylian species, reflecting the ability of large-bodied females to allocate considerable resources to reproduction without compromising somatic maintenance. Each nesting event typically involves the deposition of a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], and the eggs are buried in a mound nest constructed from vegetation and soil, where the heat of decomposition, combined with solar radiation, maintains the incubation temperature. The temperature-dependent sex determination system means that the incubation regime profoundly influences offspring sex ratios.

The maximum lifespan of Crocodylus niloticus has been documented at 90 years [am = 90 years] when individuals are maintained at a mean ambient temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], a longevity that positions this species among the longest-lived of all reptiles. This extended lifespan, combined with a late age at first reproduction and relatively low annual mortality rates once adulthood is attained, aligns with a classic slow life history strategy typical of large-bodied, top-tier predators. Very old individuals, particularly males, often exhibit substantial scarring and tooth wear, yet they continue to maintain dominance over key basking and nesting sites along river systems. This impressive longevity also permits multiple reproductive seasons over a female's lifetime, with the largest and oldest females contributing disproportionately to population recruitment due to their elevated fecundity and the superior quality of nest sites they can defend.
